newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's bank sector likely to see more upheaval.
newsitem.headline: Italy's bank sector likely to see more upheaval.

text.p: Italy's financial community is bracing itself for more upheaval after a week in which savings bank Cariplo announced plans to merge with Ambroveneto and an offer for shares in San Paolo was heavily oversubscribed.

The decision by Cariplo, which stands for Cassa di Risparmio delle Provincie Lombarde, to agree to a takeover by Ambroveneto will lead to the creation of the second biggest bank in the country, measured by deposits, after San Paolo .

It was the latest signal that a big shake-up is under way in Italy's inefficient and heavily overstaffed banking industry, which San Paolo chairman Gianni Zandano once described as "a petrified forest."

San Paolo has been at the forefront of the changes, announcing on Saturday that it had placed 220 million of its shares, worth around 2.3 trillion lire ($1.39 billion), with employees, private and institutional investors in the largest public share offering by an Italian bank.
All eyes are now on Banca Commerciale Italiana's next move after the Milan bank's offer to link up with Cariplo was spurned by the savings bank in favour of Ambroveneto.

BCI's rejection by Cariplo has been seen as a slap in the face both for the bank's management and its allies at merchant bank Mediobanca, which at one time enjoyed an unchallenged role as a mover and shaker of corporate alliances in Italy.
BCI is looking increasingly like it is losing its way as rivals push ahead aggressively with merger plans.
Banca Nazionale del Lavoro has joined forces with insurance group INA to take control of Banco di Napoli, southern Italy's largest bank.

Local rival Credito Italiano, which like BCI was privatised in the early 1990s, two years ago acquired the profitable Credito Romagnolo and is widely thought to have been more successful at cutting costs and raising profitability.
Shares in BCI fell by nearly 11 percent last week on renewed speculation that it would not wait for long before it was tempted to spend its four trillion lire cash pile on a major acquisition.
Banca di Roma, the least profitable of the country's major banks, saw its shares rise 6.54 percent during the week, fuelled by talk that BCI might make a move.
Banca di Roma's chairman Cesare Geronzi gave a non-committal response when asked by journalists about the rumours of a linkup with BCI at a business conference on Saturday.

"If the market says so, listen to the market, you cannot ask me. I known nothing of this and as for the share's performance on the stock exchange, that is the market's evaluation," Turin daily La Stampa quoted Geronzi as saying.
Geronzi said that he believed the whirlwind sweeping through Italian banking was gathering pace.
"You have to take note that the clearing away of the forest is under way and the rate of progress will be much faster than you can imagine," he added.
Two smaller banks, Banca Popolare di Milano and Banca Popolare di Novara, have also been named as possible targets for a takeover bid by BCI.
